description:
THE POINTERS

A team from 42 Málaga driven by curiosity, technology and the instinct to ask one important question:

“What could go wrong?”

We like exploring the unknown, turning complex problems into solvable challenges, and building things together. Our background in coding and project-based learning gives us a strong foundation in software development, algorithms, data, problem-solving and technology, but we believe that great missions need more than code.

We are interested in space, science, AI, data, simulation, visualization, engineering and creative technology — and especially in the intersection between them.

Our approach is simple:

Observe → Understand → Experiment → Build → Test → Learn → Repeat.

Like a real mission crew, we value collaboration over individual egos. We want to combine different skills, perspectives and ways of thinking to transform ambitious ideas into something that actually works.

We are looking for developers, data enthusiasts, scientists, engineers, designers, storytellers, researchers, space enthusiasts and creative problem-solvers. You don't need to be an expert in everything — curiosity, teamwork and the willingness to learn matter just as much.

If you are ready to think beyond the obvious, face the unexpected and build something together, there is a place for you on our crew.

Mission: Explore. Solve. Create. 🚀
summary:
Worst Case Outpost is an interactive space mission design and simulation game developed by The Pointers for NASA’s Space Mission Design Game challenge. It explores the challenges of preparing and managing a space mission through decision-making, resource management, and simulated scenarios inspired by selected environmental conditions of the Moon and Mars. Players are encouraged to consider how technical choices, limited resources, environmental constraints, and human factors influence mission operations and crew wellbeing. The project is guided by three learning levels—Junior, Mid-Level, and Senior—and two core values: environmental responsibility and the physical, mental, and emotional health of the crew. By combining exploration, experimentation, and learning by doing, it aims to make the complexity of space mission design more accessible and engaging.

The Pointers is a multidisciplinary team. We share an interest in technology, space exploration, and collaborative problem-solving. Our name draws inspiration from C programming pointers and our shared journey towards ambitious possibilities. We want to inspire more people to understand the complexity and responsibility of space exploration and learning by doing. Also, Worst Case Outpost encourages players to consider the human and environmental consequences of their decisions. Its core proposition is simple: understand, experiment, learn, and make every decision count.
details:
Worst Case Outpost

SPACE MISSION DESIGN GAME

The Pointers To A Dream That Seemed (I'm)Possible.

Project Overview
  • Project name: Space Mission Design Game
  • Team: The Pointers
  • Competition: NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026
  • Local event: Málaga, Spain
  • Product type: Interactive space mission design and simulation game
  • Development language: Kotlin
  • Initial development scope: Functional prototype
  • Main concept: Design, manage and simulate a complete space mission

The Pointers to a dream that seemed (I'm)possible.

The Pointers represents a team driven by curiosity, imagination, experimentation and the desire to turn seemingly impossible ideas into achievable projects. We believe that learning, collaboration and creativity can transform ambitious dreams into concrete experiences.

Space Mission Design Game embodies this philosophy by inviting participants to explore the complexity of space exploration through experimentation, strategic decisions and interactive learning.

Executive Summary

Worst Case Outpost is an interactive space mission design and simulation game developed in Kotlin by The Pointers for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026.The project aims to provide an engaging environment where participants can design, manage and simulate complete space missions, making engineering decisions, managing limited resources and evaluating how their choices influence mission outcomes.

Players can define mission objectives, select an environment such as the Moon or Mars, configure spacecraft and scientific instruments, distribute responsibilities and face operational challenges. Throughout the experience, decisions generate consequences that can affect other components of the mission, requiring participants to understand the trade-offs involved in real-world space mission design.

The game is conceived for different experience levels, allowing participants with varying degrees of technical knowledge to experiment, make decisions, face constraints and learn.

An additional dimension of the project is the exploration of terrestrial environments that reproduce selected conditions relevant to extraterrestrial exploration. These environments can provide scientifically contextualised scenarios for mission simulations.

The long-term vision is to develop an expandable learning and simulation experience that combines space engineering fundamentals, resource management, scientific exploration, teamwork and human factors.

Project Vision

Our vision is to make the complexity of space mission design accessible through an interactive experience that transforms theoretical knowledge into practical decisions.

Space exploration involves interconnected systems, competing priorities and limited resources. A decision concerning spacecraft mass, for example, can affect fuel requirements, launch possibilities, available instruments and the overall mission budget. Rather than presenting these concepts as isolated technical subjects, the game aims to allow participants to experience their relationships directly. Players should be able to experiment, make mistakes, discover unexpected consequences and understand why certain decisions are more suitable than others.

The long-term ambition is to create an expandable simulation experience inspired by the freedom of construction and exploration found in sandbox games, while introducing the engineering constraints, scientific reasoning and operational complexity associated with real space missions.

The experience should encourage curiosity without sacrificing scientific credibility.

Project Mission

The mission of Space Mission Design Game is to create an interactive learning environment in which participants can:

  • Understand the fundamental components of a space mission.
  • Explore different mission objectives and environments.
  • Experiment with spacecraft and mission configurations.
  • Select scientific instruments and equipment.
  • Manage limited resources and operational constraints.
  • Distribute responsibilities among crew members.
  • Make engineering and strategic decisions.
  • Experience the consequences of their choices.
  • Evaluate mission performance and survival outcomes.
  • Learn from successful and unsuccessful mission scenarios.

The experience should make participants active decision-makers rather than passive observers.

Core Experience

The central gameplay concept revolves around designing a mission and discovering whether the selected strategy can achieve its objectives.

The proposed experience includes the following elements:

  • Mission Definition: Players establish the fundamental characteristics of their mission:
    1. Destination: Moon or Mars.
    2. Selected environment or location.
    3. Mission objectives.
    4. Difficulty level.
    5. Available mission duration.
    1. Spacecraft configuration.
    2. Scientific instruments.
    3. Equipment and technology.
    4. Operational systems.
    5. Available materials and resources.
  • Resource Management: Players must work within a limited resource system. Potential constraints include: budget, mass, energy, communications, data capacity, mission duration and available equipment and materials. The availability of resources should influence the decisions players can make.
    1. Whether the mission objectives were achieved.
    2. Whether the crew survived.
    3. How efficiently resources were managed.
    4. Which decisions contributed to success or failure.
    5. Which risks were underestimated.
    6. What could be improved in another attempt.

Educational Philosophy

The educational approach is based on three fundamental principles:

Understand. Experiment. Learn.

The perspective shared by Gospel Fita, Intelligent Automation Project Coordinator at GGPEN, reinforces three important objectives:

  1. Understand the fundamentals of a space mission.
  2. Experiment and make decisions.
  3. Face limitations and learn through experience.

These principles align with the project's intention to transform space mission design into an accessible and interactive learning experience.

The game should not simply reward participants for selecting the correct answer. It should help them understand why a decision works, what compromises it involves and how it affects other mission components.

Learning through experimentation

Participants should be encouraged to:

  • Test different mission configurations.
  • Compare alternative strategies.
  • Identify limitations.
  • Understand interconnected systems.
  • Learn from failures.
  • Improve their decisions through repeated simulations.

Failure is therefore considered a potential learning outcome rather than simply a negative game result.

Adaptability and Accessibility

The game is intended for participants with different levels of knowledge and experience. Three difficulty levels are proposed:

  • Junior — Beginner: Introduces basic space mission concepts through guided decisions, accessible explanations and manageable scenarios.
  • Mid-Level — Intermediate: Introduces more interconnected constraints, independent decisions and more complex mission management situations.
  • Senior — Advanced: Introduces demanding engineering trade-offs, limited resources, complex scenarios and strategic decisions.

The objective is to make the experience accessible without removing the underlying complexity of space mission design. Difficulty should influence the complexity of the simulation, available assistance and decision-making requirements.

The Pointers’ Philosophy

Learning something complex requires more than memorising concepts. It requires understanding how things work, experimenting with possibilities, making decisions, facing mistakes and discovering how every action affects the final outcome. This is the philosophy behind Worst Case Outpost.

As students at 42 Málaga – Fundación Telefónica, we experience a learning environment built around autonomy, practical challenges, problem-solving and collaboration. We learn by doing: exploring unfamiliar problems, researching solutions, testing our ideas, making mistakes and improving through experience. Our education has taught us that knowledge becomes meaningful when we can apply it.

This is particularly relevant to space exploration. Designing a space mission is not simply a matter of understanding individual engineering concepts. It means connecting multiple systems, working with limited resources, anticipating risks and making decisions whose consequences can affect the entire mission.

Reading about these challenges can introduce the theory. Experiencing them through interactive decisions can make their complexity much easier to understand. That is what we want players to discover through Worst Case Outpost.

Rather than simply presenting information about space missions, our game invites users to take responsibility for designing and managing one. They experiment with resources, evaluate alternatives, confront operational challenges and learn from the consequences of their choices.

We believe this approach can encourage curiosity, critical thinking, scientific understanding and a more practical relationship with knowledge.

Why The Pointers?

Our team name comes from one of the fundamental concepts we study extensively in the C programming language: pointers. In C, a pointer stores the memory address of another object, allowing a program to access and work with data indirectly. Understanding pointers requires learning to think beyond the value itself: understanding where information is located, how it is accessed and how different parts of a system relate to one another.

For us, this concept became a metaphor. We are The Pointers because we see ourselves as people learning to find directions, connect ideas and navigate towards possibilities that may initially seem out of reach. Our motto captures that spirit:

The Pointers to a dream that seemed (I'm)possible.

The wordplay between impossible and I'm possible represents the transformation we experience through learning: what initially appears impossible can become achievable through curiosity, persistence, collaboration and the willingness to solve problems.

Worst Case Outpost is an expression of that philosophy. We are students learning to build technology, but we are also explorers learning to approach complex challenges with creativity and determination. And we want our players to experience that same transformation.

Understand. Experiment. Learn.

Because sometimes, the most important discovery is not the destination itself, but everything we learn while finding our way there.

Technical Architecture

Worst Case Outpost is developed in Kotlin, using the Android application development ecosystem and compatible tools for the project.  The choice of Kotlin allows building a structured application, maintaining simulation logic independent of the user interface, and facilitating future extensions.

  • Programming language: Kotlin.
  • Development environment: Android Studio.
  • Build system: Gradle.
  • Application framework: To be documented according to the project configuration
  • User interface: To be documented according to the implemented UI framework
  • Data storage: To be documented according to the implemented persistence system
  • Version control: Git and GitHub

The proposed logical architecture organizes the system into components with distinct responsibilities:

  • Presentation: interface, screens, navigation, and user interaction.
  • Domain: business rules, mission management, and simulation logic.
  • Data: access, organization, and information persistence.
  • Models: representation of missions, environments, resources, events, and crew.

This separation seeks to reduce coupling between components and facilitate product maintenance and evolution. The final structure must correspond to the modules and packages existing in the repository.

The system needs to represent the fundamental elements of a space mission:

  • Mission: Objectives, destination, and general configuration.
  • Environment: Characteristics of the simulation scenario.
  • Resource: Available resources and their quantities.
  • Crew: Members and responsibilities of the crew.
  • Equipment: Available instruments and systems.
  • Event: Events that affect the mission.
  • Decision: Player alternatives and choices.
  • Mission Result: Final state and evaluation of the mission.

These models constitute the conceptual data structure. Their correspondence with implemented classes or structures must be verified in the code. The simulation engine represents the logic connecting player decisions with changes in the mission state. Its responsibility is to process choices, apply defined rules, and communicate consequences to the interface. The architecture contemplates a modular logic that allows incorporating new variables, events, and evaluation conditions without having to rebuild the entire application.

The project contemplates using scientific information and public resources related to space exploration. Possible integrations include NASA data, information about analog environments, and scientific resources to substantiate scenarios. Each integration must document its source, purpose, format, and method of incorporation. A source is not considered integrated simply by appearing in the bibliography.

Persistence must allow storing the necessary information to maintain experience continuity. Among potentially storable data are mission configurations, resources, decisions, and results.

The storage mechanism and scope must be documented according to the effective MVP implementation.

The architecture must prioritize:

  • Modularity and separation of responsibilities.
  • Maintainable and reusable code.
  • Consistency of mission states.
  • Efficient management of data and resources.
  • Ease of testing simulation logic.
  • Possibility of incorporating new scenarios and mechanics.

In the long term, this foundation could evolve toward more complex simulations, expanded persistence, player collaboration, and integration of additional scientific sources. Technical principle: build a functional foundation first; expand complexity only when the core simulation is reliable.

Team Responsibilities

The distribution of responsibilities includes the following areas:

  • @asierra: Data, Design/UX, Communication
  • @aternero: Design/UX, Communication, Organization
  • @cacortes: Design/UX, Communication
  • @mmorente: Programming, Data, Science
  • @sternero: Programming, Data, Science, Organization

Shared responsibilities allow combining technical, scientific, organizational, and creative perspectives.

Team coordination focuses on maintaining a common product vision and prioritizing high-impact tasks.

Work principles include:

  • Define concrete goals.
  • Divide work into manageable tasks.
  • Maintain continuous communication.
  • Share progress and blockers.
  • Review design and development decisions.
  • Prioritize integration over isolated work.
  • Document relevant changes.

Development prioritizes three levels:

  1. Core functionality: indispensable elements to demonstrate the main concept.
  2. Experience improvements: usability, clarity, and learning enhancements.
  3. Future expansion: advanced features outside the initial scope.

This prioritization allows concentrating time and resources on demonstrating the essential product value. Development principle: build what matters, validate what works and expand what proves valuable.

References and Credits

NASA and Scientific References

The project takes as its starting point the official Space Mission Design Game challenge and uses research on terrestrial analog environments as reference to contextualize scenarios.

  • NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026: Official framework of the competition and context of the challenge.
  • NASA – Historical Sounds: Inversive sounds to enhance the user experience.
  • NASA – Images: Images to make the app's design more appealing.

These sources ground the conceptual and scientific context of the project. Their inclusion does not imply that their databases, images, or APIs are integrated into the prototype.

Related NASA Challenges

Other NASA challenges have also been considered as references to identify relevant space exploration concerns:

  • Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer: inspiration for adapting the experience to different learning levels.
  • Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars: connection to selecting and understanding analog terrestrial environments.
  • Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions: consideration of physical and human crew wellbeing.
  • Abandoned but not Forgotten: reflection on managing, reusing, and responsibly taking advantage of equipment.

These challenges are used as complementary references. They do not replace the main challenge nor imply that their solutions are implemented in Worst Case Outpost.

Development Tools and Technologies

Project tools and technologies must be documented according to their effective use.

  • Kotlin: Programming language of the project.
  • Android Studio: Development environment.
  • Gradle: Project management and build system.
  • GitHub: Version control and code publishing.
  • NASA Open Resources: Scientific and contextual information query, according to resources effectively used.

Dependencies, libraries, design tools, and additional external resources must be incorporated into the record when their use is confirmed.

Artificial Intelligence Disclosure

Artificial intelligence was used as support during the ideation and documentation phase.

Its contribution includes:

  • Exploring possible design approaches.
  • Organizing and structuring ideas.
  • Generating initial proposals.
  • Support in drafting and project communication.

Use of ChatGPT (OpenAI)

AI-generated contributions are considered support material, not scientific sources or evidence of implemented features. The team maintains responsibility for reviewing, cross-checking, adapting, and validating project content and decisions. AI tools used must be identified by name and purpose in the final version of this section.

ChatGPT was used as an AI-assisted support tool throughout the conceptualisation, research, planning and documentation of Worst Case Outpost, developed by The Pointers for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026.

Its contributions included:

  1. Research and Information Support
    1. Supporting the exploration of the NASA challenge and related space exploration topics.
    2. Helping identify relevant NASA resources and scientific references.
    3. Providing explanations of planetary analog environments, mission design concepts and space exploration constraints.
    4. Suggesting related NASA challenges that could inform the project's broader perspective.
    1. Helping structure and refine the project's vision, mission, objectives and value proposition.
    2. Exploring potential gameplay mechanics, resource management systems and mission simulation concepts.
    3. Suggesting possible educational applications and future development opportunities.
    1. Assisting in the organisation and drafting of the 13 sections of the project documentation.
    2. Supporting the description of proposed user experiences, system architecture, development methodology, testing strategies and project deliverables.
    3. Helping distinguish between implemented functionality, conceptual proposals and future development possibilities.
    1. Improving the clarity, consistency and professional presentation of project descriptions.
    2. Supporting the development of concise explanations of the project's purpose, educational value and relevance to the NASA challenge.
    3. Assisting with the organisation of information for project communication and evaluation.

Human Responsibility and Authorship

ChatGPT did not independently develop, program, execute or test the Worst Case Outpost application, nor did it make decisions on behalf of the team.

The Pointers retain responsibility for the project's concept, creative direction, implementation, technical decisions, verification of information, selection of resources and final deliverables.

AI-generated suggestions and content have been treated as supporting material, subject to human review, adaptation and validation.

ChatGPT served as an AI-assisted collaborator for research, conceptual development and documentation. The project itself remains the responsibility and work of The Pointers.

Code, Images and Third-Party Materials

Any external resource incorporated into the product or its presentation must have an identifiable reference.

The registry must include:

  • Resource or material name.
  • Author, organization, or responsible entity.
  • Source URL.
  • Resource type: code, image, text, data, or tool.
  • License and terms of use, where applicable.
  • Modifications made by the team.

Open resources and materials allowed under their respective licenses will be prioritized. Original materials developed by The Pointers must be identified as proprietary production.

Team Credits

The Pointers is a multidisciplinary team of programming students from 42 Málaga – Fundación Telefónica.

  • @asierra: Data, Design/UX, Communication
  • @aternero: Design/UX, Communication, Organization
  • @cacortes: Design/UX, Communication
  • @mmorente: Programming, Data, Science
  • @sternero: Programming, Data, Science, Organization

Team motto:
The Pointers to a dream that seemed (I'm)possible.

Project Repository

Source code: The Pointers – NASA Space Apps 2026

The repository constitutes the point of reference for consulting technical development, project structure, and team contributions. Final documentation must include execution instructions, requirements, dependencies, and applicable licenses to facilitate review.

Attribution and Transparency

The Pointers acknowledges external sources, tools, technologies, and contributions that supported the development of Worst Case Outpost. Transparency regarding resource origins and actual utilization scope is part of the team's commitment to quality, responsibility, and project reproducibility. Our work is built on curiosity, collaboration and responsible use of knowledge.
